questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five short functions, two of them binding a name inside a condition and three of them taking a path apart without touching a disk.

How this works in Python

Assigning inside a condition

Java treats assignment as an expression, so an assignment can sit inside a condition and hand its value straight to the test.

String line;
while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
    lines.add(line);
}

Python treats = as a statement, so that shape has never compiled. Write while (value = step(value)) > 0: and you get a SyntaxError. The language refused the feature for twenty-six years, because = inside a condition is usually a typo for ==.

Python 3.8 added a separate operator for the job, :=. It is called the walrus operator, after the animal its two eyes and tusks resemble. It binds a name and gives back the same value in one breath.

while (value := value // 2) > 0:
    steps.append(value)

The name outlives the loop, exactly as an ordinary for variable does. Nothing about scope changes. The only thing the walrus buys you is the right to bind where an expression is expected, and Python still refuses a bare = there, so the typo it was guarding against cannot get through.

The second place it earns its keep

A comprehension filter often computes the very thing the output expression wants. Without the walrus you compute it twice.

[PurePosixPath(p).name for p in paths if PurePosixPath(p).suffix == ".csv"]

That builds every path object twice, and a reader has to compare the two calls character by character to be sure they agree. Bind it in the filter and the output reads it back.

[pure.name for p in paths if (pure := PurePosixPath(p)).suffix == ".csv"]

The filter runs before the output expression, so the name is bound by the time the front of the comprehension asks for it.

Where it hurts

Those two positions are the whole of it. Everywhere else the walrus costs a reader more than it saves you. A binding buried in the middle of a long expression is invisible to somebody scanning the left margin for the place a name was born, and two walruses in one expression turn a line into a puzzle. A plain assignment on its own line is free and says the same thing.

total = (subtotal := price * count) + (tax := subtotal * 0.15)   # do not
return (result := compute(x))                                    # pointless

Pure paths

Java hands you two path types with different habits. File mixes path arithmetic with disk access, so new File(dir, name).exists() both builds a path and goes to the disk. Path is better behaved and knows its own parts.

Path p = Paths.get("/var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv");
p.getParent();               // /var/log
p.getFileName();             // raw_sensor_07.csv
p.resolve("processed");      // /var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv/processed

Java stops there. It has no accessor for the part before the dot and none for the extension, so everybody writes the same lastIndexOf('.') arithmetic and one of them gets it wrong.

Python's pathlib splits the two habits into separate types. Path talks to the disk. PurePosixPath does path arithmetic and nothing else, so it never checks whether anything exists and never raises because a directory is missing. Every function below uses the pure kind.

pure = PurePosixPath("/var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv")
pure.parent      # PurePosixPath('/var/log')
pure.name        # 'raw_sensor_07.csv'
pure.stem        # 'raw_sensor_07'
pure.suffix      # '.csv'

Four accessors, and the last two are the ones Java made you compute.

/var/log / raw_sensor_07 .csv
--------   ------------- ----
parent     stem          suffix
           --------------------
           name

Two more pieces finish the set. with_suffix(".json") returns a new path with the extension swapped, and adds one when the name had none. Only the last suffix moves, so a.tar.gz becomes a.tar.json.

The / operator joins, in place of resolve. Python lets a class decide what its operators mean, which you met in the dunders and dataclasses topic, and pathlib spends that freedom on the character every path already contains.

PurePosixPath("/var/log") / "processed" / "p1.csv"
# PurePosixPath('/var/log/processed/p1.csv')

A pure path prints as PurePosixPath('/var/log') rather than as text, so a function handing one back to a caller who wants a string wraps it in str(...).

Your task

The answer box imports PurePosixPath for you. Write five functions.

  • halve_steps(value) halves a whole number over and over, and returns every value it passes through on the way down. Halve with //, stop as soon as the result reaches zero, and keep the zero out of the list. Bind the new value in the while condition.
  • csv_names(paths) takes a list of path strings and returns the name of every path whose suffix is ".csv". One comprehension, and the path object is built once, in the filter.
  • parts_of(path) returns the four parts of one path as a single string, in the order parent, name, stem, suffix, separated by " | ". For "/var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv" that is "/var/log | raw_sensor_07.csv | raw_sensor_07 | .csv".
  • as_json(path) returns the same path as a string with its suffix replaced by ".json".
  • joined(folder, name) returns folder and name joined into one path string.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Use the walrus in halve_steps and in csv_names, and nowhere else. A hidden test reads all five functions and fails you for a walrus in the other three.
  • Touch no file. Pure path operations only, so no open, no exists and no mkdir.
  • Do not take a path apart with split, rfind or os.path. Four accessors and the / operator cover every case here.
  • Annotate every signature, parameters and return alike.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

import inspect
mine = {name: inspect.getsource(f) for name, f in (("halve_steps", halve_steps), ("csv_names", csv_names), ("parts_of", parts_of), ("as_json", as_json), ("joined", joined))} whole = "".join(mine.values()) for banned in ("os.path", "open(", ".exists(", ".mkdir(", ".split(", "rfind(", "rsplit("): assert banned not in whole, f"rule broken: {banned} has no place in this answer" assert ":=" in mine["halve_steps"], "rule broken: halve_steps wants a walrus" assert "while " in mine["halve_steps"], "rule broken: bind the new value in a while condition" assert ":=" in mine["csv_names"], "rule broken: csv_names wants a walrus" assert "append(" not in mine["csv_names"], "rule broken: csv_names is one comprehension" for quiet in ("parts_of", "as_json", "joined"): assert ":=" not in mine[quiet], f"rule broken: no walrus in {quiet}, it buys nothing there" for name, func in (("halve_steps", halve_steps), ("csv_names", csv_names), ("parts_of", parts_of), ("as_json", as_json), ("joined", joined)): hints = func.__annotations__ missing = [p for p in inspect.signature(func).parameters if p not in hints] assert not missing, f"rule broken: annotate {name}, missing {missing}" assert "return" in hints, f"rule broken: annotate the return type of {name}"
print(halve_steps(0), halve_steps(3), csv_names([])) print(as_json("notes"), parts_of("t1.csv")) print(joined(".", "p1.csv"), as_json("logs/a.tar.gz"))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Rewrite four generic functions, one generic container class and two type aliases in the bracket syntax Python 3.12 added.

How this works in Python

Java declares a type parameter in angle brackets, in front of the thing it belongs to. The parameter is scoped to that method or that class, and a bound narrows what it accepts.

static <T> Optional<T> first(List<T> items) { ... }

class Stack<T> { void push(T item) { ... } }

static <T extends Comparable<T>> T largest(List<T> values) { ... }

Python asked for the same idea in a shape nothing else in the language uses. You imported TypeVar, assigned one to a module-level name, repeated its own name as a string argument, and inherited from Generic to make a class generic.

from typing import Generic, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def first(items: list[T]) -> T | None:
    ...


class Stack(Generic[T]):
    ...

That spelling still runs and you will meet it in any codebase older than a year, so recognise it. Do not write it. Python 3.12 added the bracket syntax, and new code uses that.

def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T | None:
    ...


class Stack[T]:
    ...

The brackets go where Java puts its angle brackets, and they read the same way. The type parameter is scoped to that one function or class, so two functions writing [T] no longer share a module-level object, and the name never has to be repeated as a string.

The third piece is the type statement, which declares a type alias, a name for a type you would rather not spell out at every use.

type Channel = tuple[str, float]
type Result[T] = T | None

A plain Channel = tuple[str, float] assignment gives you a variable that happens to hold a type. The type statement gives you an alias object that a type checker recognises as one, and an alias takes its own parameters in brackets. The right-hand side is evaluated lazily, so an alias may name a class defined further down the file.

A bare [T] accepts anything. Two spellings narrow it. A bound written [T: Sized] says T must be that type or a subtype of it, and it is the counterpart of Java's extends. Constraints written [T: (int, float)] say T is exactly one of those listed types and never a subtype and never a mixture, which Java has no direct equivalent for. Reach for a bound when you need a capability, and for constraints when you mean a closed set.

None of this is enforced while the program runs, which is the type hints topic again. Python records the type parameters on __type_params__ and evaluates the bound only when something asks for it. A list of strings goes into total and comes out the far side, and only the type checker objects.

Your task

The answer box holds the old spelling between two banners. Delete it and write the replacement.

  • first(items) returns the first item or None for an empty list.
  • widest(items) takes anything with a length and returns the longest item, or None for an empty list. Bind its type parameter to Sized from collections.abc.
  • total(values) adds a non-empty list of numbers and returns the total. Constrain its type parameter to int and float.
  • apply_all(items, func) takes two type parameters and returns [func(item) for item in items]. Annotate func with Callable from collections.abc.
  • Stack is a generic container. push adds and returns nothing, pop removes and returns the last item, peek returns the last item or None, __len__ returns the count and __iter__ walks the items oldest first.
  • Result and Channel are the two aliases. Result takes one parameter and means that type or None. Channel means tuple[str, float].

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write def f[T]() and class Stack[T]. The old TypeVar spelling is banned, and so is the Generic[T] base class.
  • Declare each alias with the type statement. A plain assignment gives you a variable, not an alias.
  • Say what each type parameter allows. widest needs a length, and total takes int or float and nothing else.
  • Return T | None from first. No sentinel string, no -1, no exception.
  • Annotate every signature. Parameters and return type, no exceptions.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

name.text: WAT 23.3: The Walrus and the Path!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that replace an old-style summariser with dict merging, pure paths, prefix trimming, batching and the walrus.

How this works in Python

This tier gathers the additions that arrived between Python 3.8 and 3.12, the ones a tutorial written in 2019 cannot mention. Each one has a Java habit behind it. The walrus and pure paths come back from the first tier of this topic, with three more additions beside them.

Java lets you assign inside a condition, and every reader of that language knows the shape.

String line;
while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
    lines.add(line);
}

Python refused for twenty-six years, because = in a condition is usually a typo for ==. Python 3.8 added a separate operator for it, :=, called the walrus operator after the animal it resembles. It binds a name and gives back the value in the same breath.

while (value := next(source, None)) is not None:
    kept.append(value)

Compare against a sentinel with is not None rather than truthiness, because 0.0 and "" are falsey and a reading of zero is still a reading. The other place the walrus earns its keep is a comprehension whose filter computes something the output needs, so the work happens once instead of twice.

[code for line in lines if (code := line.removeprefix("ERR-")) != line]

It hurts everywhere else. A walrus in a plain return, or a second one in the same expression, buries the binding where a reader scanning the left margin will not find it. Use it in those two positions and nowhere else.

Java gives you Paths.get and a Path that knows its own parts. Python's equivalent is pathlib, and its PurePosixPath does path arithmetic without touching a disk. parent, name, stem and suffix take a path apart, with_suffix() replaces the extension, and / joins.

pure = PurePosixPath("/var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv")
pure.parent      # PurePosixPath('/var/log')
pure.name        # 'raw_sensor_07.csv'
pure.stem        # 'raw_sensor_07'
pure.suffix      # '.csv'
str(pure.parent / "processed" / pure.stem)   # '/var/log/processed/raw_sensor_07'

Trimming a fixed prefix by hand is where off-by-one defects breed. base[4:] is correct until somebody edits the prefix and forgets the number, and base[:-4] silently eats four characters off a name that never had the suffix. Python 3.9 added str.removeprefix and str.removesuffix, which take the text itself and return the string unchanged when it does not match.

Python 3.9 also gave dicts the | operator. defaults | overrides returns a new merged dict with the right-hand side winning, and it leaves both operands alone. config |= overrides updates in place instead, so a function doing that returns None and its annotation says -> None.

Python 3.12 added itertools.batched. batched(readings, 3) yields tuples of three, and the last tuple is short when the input does not divide evenly. It replaces the accumulator loop that everyone writes slightly differently.

Your task

The answer box holds summarise_old, a function written the way all of this used to be written. Leave it alone. The tests run it beside yours and compare, so it is the oracle you have to match.

  • summarise(paths, readings, defaults, overrides, size) returns a dict with three keys. "settings" is defaults merged under overrides. "names" is one name per path, taken from the last path segment with "raw_" off the front and ".csv" off the end. "groups" is the readings in tuples of size.
  • output_path(source, folder) takes "/var/log/raw_sensor_07.csv" and "processed" and returns the string "/var/log/processed/sensor_07.json". Drop "raw_", put the file in folder beside its old parent, and give it a .json suffix.
  • apply_overrides(config, overrides) updates config in place and returns nothing.
  • drain(source) pulls every float out of an iterator and returns them in a list. Stop on the sentinel, not on truthiness.
  • flagged(lines) returns the code from every line starting "ERR-", with that prefix removed, and skips every other line.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not build a path with string concatenation, str.split or os.path.join. PurePosixPath and / do the job.
  • Touch no file. Pure path operations only, so no open, no exists and no mkdir.
  • Slice no string to trim a prefix or a suffix. removeprefix and removesuffix are exact and never off by one.
  • Merge with | and update with |=. A loop over overrides is banned.
  • Use the walrus in drain and in flagged, and nowhere else. A walrus that saves nobody a line is a defect waiting for a reader in a hurry.
  • Annotate every signature. Parameters and return type, no exceptions.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.
